name: Walking pad
lead: A walking pad is a slim, low-speed folding treadmill, usually without handrails, designed to slide under a desk, sofa or bed. Speeds on consumer models commonly top out at about 6 km/h, well below the roughly 0 to 20 km/h range described for professional fitness treadmills [1]. It is used to add steady walking to desk-based days, often while working or watching television.

In appearance-oriented communities the walking pad is discussed as a way to increase daily steps and energy expenditure and to reduce sitting time, supporting leanness. No published trial has tested walking pads as a product. The closest research concerns treadmill desks and other active workstations, which have been the subject of several systematic reviews.

A 2021 meta-analysis of 13 treadmill-desk studies (351 participants) found that laboratory studies showed an increase in energy expenditure of about 105 kcal per hour compared with sitting, and that workplace studies showed a small reduction in sitting time of about 1.7 minutes per hour over 24 hours, with no significant differences in blood pressure [2]. Other reviews describe mixed effects on psychological well-being and work performance [3][4].
infobox: First consumer home treadmill, the PaceMaster 600, developed by William Staub in the late 1960s [1]

paras: Treadmills in general consist of a moving belt driven by an electric motor on which the user walks or runs in place [1]. Walking pads simplify this design with a lower maximum speed, a thinner folding frame and, commonly, a remote control instead of a console and handrails, so that they can be stored flat. Safety standards for treadmills generally, such as IEC EN 957, apply to fitness treadmills sold in Europe [1], though the specific compliance of low-cost walking pads varies by product.

Walking pads are marketed alongside standing desks. Research has examined treadmill desks, in which a standard treadmill is paired with a raised desk, and the results are generally taken as the nearest guide to walking-pad use [2][5].

Treadmills began as human- and animal-powered treadwheels used for work, and later in 19th-century prisons as a form of penal labour. One source credits the engineer William Cubitt with inventing the penal treadwheel in 1818 [6]. The first patent for an exercise treadmill machine in the United States was issued in 1913, and Robert Bruce and Wayne Quinton developed a treadmill for cardiac testing at the University of Washington in 1952 [1]. William Staub made the first consumer treadmill for home use, the PaceMaster 600, after reading Kenneth Cooper's 1968 book Aerobics [1].

Slow, desk-oriented treadmills developed from the active-workstation research of the 2000s and 2010s, with randomized trials of treadmill desks published from 2013 [7]. The specific walking-pad product category, which consumer-electronics firms sold as compact under-desk machines, has no detailed history in the sources reviewed.

In laboratory studies pooled in the 2021 meta-analysis, treadmill-desk users expended about 105 kcal more per hour and had a higher metabolic rate than when sitting [2]. In workplace studies, sitting time fell by a small amount over 24 hours [2]. A 2015 systematic review found that treadmill desks produced the largest physiological improvements among standing and treadmill desks, including postprandial glucose, HDL cholesterol and anthropometrics, and that psychological and work-performance outcomes were mixed [4]. A review of active workstations in people with overweight or obesity reported that the treadmill desk was the only workstation for which improvements in body weight management measures were reported, alongside reductions in sedentary time and improved glycaemic control [5].

Reviews of work performance found that sit-stand desks had no detrimental effect, whereas some studies of treadmill and cycling workstations identified possible decreases in some cognitive task performance, and that many studies were underpowered [8]. A 2019 meta-analysis of interventions to reduce sedentary behaviour in people with overweight or obesity also addressed the topic more broadly [9].

Wikipedia's general treadmill entry notes that treadmills can cause injury if used improperly, with particular concern about children reaching into a moving belt, and recommends removing the safety key when not in use [1]. It also lists noise and vibration, space, cost and repairs as disadvantages [1]. Hobbyist reviews of low-cost walking pads sometimes discuss motor overheating, noise and weight-limit accuracy, though these are product-level reports rather than research findings. Walking while typing or using a mouse can affect precision, and studies of treadmill and cycling workstations have reported some decrements in cognitive tasks [8].

No studies found on walking pads specifically. Treadmill-desk research is the closest category. A 2021 meta-analysis pooled 13 studies [2]. Randomized trials include a 24-week crossover trial in 20 overweight and obese physicians [7], a 12-month cluster-randomized trial of sit-to-stand and treadmill desks in 66 overweight office workers [10], a randomized trial of a workplace treadmill-desk intervention [11], and a one-year prospective trial of treadmill desks [12]. A randomized trial also reported that reducing prolonged sitting with a treadmill desk acutely improved cardiometabolic risk markers in men and women [13]. These studies mostly used treadmills with desks, speeds and training designs that differ from commercial walking pads.

Walking pads are discussed in fitness and appearance forums as a low-effort way to add steps during remote work, with the usual framing that more daily movement supports fat loss when combined with diet. Threads on women's fitness forums ask whether they are worthwhile. Community-specific content was limited in the material reviewed.
